Association-rule mining searches for items that frequently occur together and then evaluates candidate rules using support, confidence, and lift.

Regularization discourages unnecessarily complex models by adding a penalty to the learning objective, which can reduce overfitting.

Before selecting a model, define the practical error costs, choose matching evaluation metrics, and compare all candidates on the same data split.

Suppose a bank wants to predict whether a customer will repay a loan. The model can use income, existing debt, repayment history, and employment stability, but it must not learn from information recorded after the lending decision. We therefore define a clear prediction timestamp, remove future information, split the data chronologically, and evaluate both discrimination and calibration before deployment.

A decision tree starts with all training examples at the root node. It evaluates possible feature splits and chooses the one that produces the greatest reduction in impurity. The same procedure continues recursively in each child node. If the tree grows without restriction, it may fit noise, so maximum depth, minimum leaf size, or pruning is used to control complexity.

In K-means clustering, the requested number of clusters must be chosen in advance. The algorithm initializes centroids, assigns each observation to its nearest centroid, recomputes each centroid from its assigned observations, and repeats. Because different initializations can produce different solutions, we run the method several times and retain the solution with the lowest within-cluster variation.

The silhouette value for one observation combines cohesion and separation. Cohesion measures the average distance to other observations in the same cluster. Separation measures the lowest average distance to observations in another cluster. Values near one indicate a suitable assignment, values near zero indicate an observation near a boundary, and negative values suggest that another cluster may fit better.

A classifier can achieve high accuracy and still be useless when the positive class is rare. Imagine that only one percent of transactions are fraudulent. A model predicting every transaction as legitimate reaches ninety-nine percent accuracy but detects no fraud. We therefore inspect recall, precision, the precision-recall curve, and the operational cost of missed cases and false alerts.

Cross-validation provides several estimates of model performance rather than relying on one fortunate split. The training data is divided into folds, the model is trained on all but one fold, and evaluation is performed on the held-out fold. This rotates until every fold has been held out. Preprocessing must be fitted inside each training fold to prevent data leakage.

Association rules describe relationships such as customers who buy one item also tending to buy another. Support measures how often the complete item set appears. Confidence estimates how often the consequent appears when the antecedent appears. Lift compares that confidence with the consequent's baseline frequency. A high-confidence rule can still be uninformative when the consequent is already very common.

Principal component analysis can reduce dimensionality when variables are correlated. First, the features are centered and often standardized. The method then finds orthogonal directions ordered by the amount of variance they explain. We choose enough components to preserve an acceptable share of variation, but we also inspect interpretability because each component is a weighted combination of the original variables.

A production model should be monitored after deployment because the world can change. Input distributions may drift, labels may arrive late, and the relationship between features and outcomes may weaken. Monitoring should cover data quality, prediction distributions, latency, failures, and performance once labels become available. Alerts should lead to investigation rather than automatic retraining without review.

Missing data requires more than replacing every blank value with a mean. We first ask why values are missing and whether missingness itself carries information. Numerical and categorical variables may need different treatments. The imputation method must be learned only from training data, applied consistently to validation and test data, and packaged with the model for identical processing during inference.

When comparing two models, use the same evaluation dataset and report uncertainty rather than focusing on one score. A small average improvement may disappear across different samples, while a modest accuracy loss may be acceptable if latency, interpretability, or fairness improves substantially. The final choice should reflect the real decision cost and the constraints of the environment where predictions are used.
